source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng 11:e88053)
finding: Only direct test found of Klein's RPD as a prompt. Two NDM prompts (RPD, data-frame) raised overall triage accuracy a little over a default prompt across 10 OpenAI models.
numbers: 45 real vignettes x 10 models x 3 prompts x 10 runs = 13,500 answers. Overall accuracy: default 63.3% (CI 61.9-64.7), RPD 67.6% (66.3-69.0), data-frame 66.7% (65.3-68.0). Mixed logistic model: RPD OR 2.26, z 8.69; data-frame OR 2.05, z 7.23; both P<.001.
limits: Single domain (self-triage). No human users. Only OpenAI models. Gain is about 4 points. No control prompt of equal length such as plain chain of thought, so the gain may come from any reasoning text.
agent_relevance: RPD as a scaffold gives a small but measurable lift. Treat it as one candidate generate-and-test operator, not a mode switch. Always compare against a plain think-step-by-step arm.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng 11:e88053)
finding: How RPD was turned into a prompt: match the case to a typical known case, state the usual decision, simulate it, test whether it works, modify and retest if it fails; if unfamiliar, reassess until it feels familiar.
numbers: Output format 'Analysis ... || Answer ...'. Data-frame prompt: build a frame, elaborate it, question it for inconsistencies, preserve or reframe, compare alternative frames. Default prompt asked only 'Answer: [category]' with no reasoning.
limits: The 'feels familiar' step has no meaning for a model without a felt sense; it is a text instruction only. The default arm has no reasoning at all, so RPD vs default mixes 'any reasoning' with 'RPD reasoning'.
agent_relevance: The RPD loop (typical case, simulate, test, repair) maps onto our generate-test operators. The recognition step must be backed by retrieved cases, not by a feeling.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng 11:e88053)
finding: Gain is concentrated in one class. Emergency and non-emergency cases did not move. Self-care roughly doubled.
numbers: Self-care (n=13): default 13.4% (11.6-15.4), RPD 29.8% (27.3-32.3), data-frame 24.6% (22.3-27.1). Emergency (n=2): 100 / 98 / 99%. Non-emergency (n=30): 82.5 / 82.0 / 82.8%. Overtriage was 88% of errors, undertriage 12%.
limits: Only 2 emergency cases, so no safety claim is possible. The default prompt was biased toward over-cautious answers; the NDM prompts mainly shifted that bias.
agent_relevance: The lift looks like bias correction (less over-caution), not better reasoning. Our gates must check whether a scaffold changes the prior rather than the skill.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng 11:e88053)
finding: Per-model results are very uneven. Weaker models gained most. The newest family tested (GPT-5.2) did not gain at all and slightly lost.
numbers: Overall accuracy default/RPD/data-frame: GPT-4.1 mini 49.8/60.7/62.4 (data-frame +13 pts, CI 9.7-16.1); GPT-4.1 64.4/72.7/72.4; GPT-4o 65.3/70.7/66.2; o3 70.7/75.1/76.2; GPT-5.2 Instant 57.8/56.4/55.3; GPT-5.2 Thinking 52.0/53.1/51.8. Self-care for GPT-5.2 Instant 0.0/3.1/0.0, Thinking 0.8/0.0/0.8.
limits: The authors give no tested reason for the GPT-5.2 null. Model version is confounded with collection date (Feb 2026 vs May 2025 for older models), so drift is possible.
agent_relevance: A scaffold effect can vanish across model versions. Our schema needs a per-model re-test before keeping an operator (supports our 'test first' marks).

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng 11:e88053)
finding: Reasoning models still gained from the prompts, with a positive interaction in the regression, but the largest absolute gains were for small non-reasoning models.
numbers: Reasoning-model interaction: RPD OR 2.15 (z 4.05, P<.001); data-frame OR 1.70 (z 2.65, P=.008). Reasoning models start higher: o3 default 70.7%, GPT-5.1 Thinking 70.7%. Absolute gain with RPD: o3 +4.4 pts, GPT-4.1 mini +10.9 pts.
limits: Interaction is on odds ratios; absolute gains differ by model. Gains computed from the paper's per-model table.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a scaffold is redundant on reasoning models; measure it.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng 11:e88053)
finding: Case-level view: the prompts help on some cases and hurt on others, so the mean hides a trade.
numbers: RPD raised accuracy in 18/45 cases (40%; median +18%, IQR 5-24) and lowered it in 13 (29%; median -5%, IQR 2-7). Data-frame: up in 17, down in 12. 12 of 13 RPD decreases were non-emergency cases.
limits: Each case has 100 answers per prompt (10 models x 10 runs), so small case effects are noisy.
agent_relevance: Scaffolds are not free: about 3 in 10 cases get worse. Our loop needs a check that can veto the scaffold's answer.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng 11:e88053)
finding: Output variability: NDM prompts made answers somewhat less consistent but more likely to contain the right answer at least once.
numbers: Median Fleiss kappa: default 0.766, RPD 0.717, data-frame 0.751 (not significant; RPD z=1.50 P=.13). Mean share of modal answer: 76.9 / 66.9 / 71.1%. Correct at least once in 10 runs: 73.1 / 82.2 / 78.4%.
limits: Kappa difference not significant. 'Correct at least once' is an oracle measure, unusable without a checker.
agent_relevance: RPD-style prompting widens the candidate set. That fits generate-then-test with a checker (G2/G3) but not single-shot answers.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) preprint version of the same triage study (JMIR Preprints 88053), via search-result summary
finding: The earlier preprint reported larger gains than the published paper from the same design.
numbers: Preprint (per search snippet): RPD 70.2%, data-frame 70.1%, default 64.7% overall; self-care 18.5% to 37.6%. Published: 67.6 / 66.7 / 63.3; self-care 13.4% to 29.8%.
limits: Second-hand from a search snippet; the preprint page was not readable. The snippet said six models, the published paper has ten, which may explain the shrink.
agent_relevance: Early prompt-effect estimates shrink when more models are added. Expect our own early gains to shrink too.

source: Fan, Sun, McNeese, Yen (about 2009) RPD-enabled agents (R-CAST) in multi-context C2 team decision making, IEEE SMC-A
finding: Older AI system built directly on RPD. R-CAST agents run a recognition cycle with expectancy monitoring and relevant-cue information exchange, and act as teammates in command-and-control teams.
numbers: 10 human-human (HH) teams of 2 US Army ROTC students vs 10 human-agent (HA) teams of 1 student plus 2 R-CAST agents; 3 context-switching speeds x 3 task complexities. The paper cites Klein for 'over 95% of human decisions conform to RPD in time-stressed settings' (second-hand, not checked).
limits: Small teams; students not field experts; simulated task with rules written from domain experts. Year taken from the file name.
agent_relevance: Shows an RPD engine works as a component when experience (cases) is hand-built. Our agent's case library is model memory plus retrieved precedents.

source: Fan et al. (about 2009) R-CAST experiment results
finding: Human-agent teams beat human-only teams at every time-stress level. Both degrade as stress rises, so agents shift the curve up but do not remove the stress effect.
numbers: Average Performance Index (API), HH teams at low/medium/high context switching: 4.748 / 3.208 / 2.015. HA teams: 5.725 / 3.863 / 2.833. ANOVA team type F=5.99, p=0.025; switch frequency F=169.44 and task complexity F=247.78 (both p<0.001); team type x switch interaction p=0.583.
limits: 10 teams per arm; no replication found. Agents carried hand-built rules.
agent_relevance: The helper added about +1.0 API at low and +0.8 at high stress. Time pressure still dominated, so mode choice alone does not remove load.

source: Fan, Sun, McNeese, Yen (2005) Extending the Recognition-Primed Decision Model to Support Human-Agent Collaboration (AAMAS 2005)
finding: First R-CAST test: agents as decision aids under rising time pressure. Pure-human teams fell sharply as tasks sped up; human-agent teams held up better.
numbers: 6 human teams vs 6 human-agent teams, 9 scenarios with task speed 0.2 to 1 of maximum. Human-agent better in the S3 role (p<=0.001); the S4 role difference was not significant (p=0.211).
limits: Graduate students, 6 teams per arm. Gain in only one of two roles.
agent_relevance: The strongest AI-RPD evidence is for speed-stressed teamwork, not for solo reasoning quality.

source: Norling, Sonenberg, Ronnquist; RPD integrated into BDI agents (as cited by Fan et al. and a patent summary)
finding: RPD was added to BDI agents so simulated humans act more realistically. Seen only in passing; the primary paper was not opened.
numbers: No numbers found.
limits: Second-hand via search snippet. Not verified.
agent_relevance: RPD has long been treated as a plan-library selection rule: retrieve plan, check expectancy, switch. The same shape as our state router.

source: Mainali et al. (2025) Classical AI vs. LLMs for Decision-Maker Alignment in Health Insurance Choices, arXiv:2510.06093
finding: Compares a classical AI decision maker (case-based reasoning, Bayesian reasoning, naturalistic decision-making, from a DARPA-style triage line) with GPT-5 and GPT-4 using weighted self-consistency. Alignment was equal.
numbers: Overall alignment accuracy: classical AI 0.892, GPT-5 (reasoning) 0.895, GPT-4 0.892. Three synthetic targets with risk tolerance 0.0, 0.5, 1.0. Classical AI slightly better on the moderate (0.5) target.
limits: Synthetic targets, small dataset, single run per setup (authors say future work will average over iterations). Differences of 0.003 are noise.
agent_relevance: An NDM-style classical system and zero-shot LLMs tie on matching a decision maker's style. Precedent retrieval is not clearly better than a prompted LLM here.

source: Zheng, Miller, Bialkowski, Soyer, Janda (2025) Supporting Data-Frame Dynamics in AI-assisted Decision Making, arXiv:2504.15894
finding: Formalizes Klein's data-frame theory as three functions: evidence extraction, hypothesis retrieval, hypothesis scoring in [0,1], looped until the best hypothesis passes a threshold.
numbers: Formal model: stop when the maximum score over hypotheses is at least tau; otherwise add evidence or add hypotheses. Demo: skin-cancer prototype with a concept bottleneck model. No user study, no numbers.
limits: Position paper at a workshop (AIREASONING 2025), no measured result.
agent_relevance: A ready spec for a data-frame loop: extract, retrieve frames, score, expand on failure. Maps onto our operators with the threshold as a code-checked gate.

source: Jain & Khurana (2025) Collaborative Causal Sensemaking, arXiv:2512.07801 (AAMAS 2026)
finding: Argues LLM agents are trained as answer engines and lack the collaborative sensemaking experts use (cites Klein's Sources of Power and data-frame). Names sycophancy as fatal for sensemaking, which needs repair of mental models.
numbers: 6-page position paper. No experiments. Cites studies on automation bias and verification overhead.
limits: Agenda paper only; no measurement.
agent_relevance: Warns that a sycophantic model cannot play the 'question the frame' role. Our frame challenge must come from code or a separate check, not from the model agreeing.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths (2025) Mind Your Step (by Step): CoT can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse (ICML 2025)
finding: Direct machine test of the 'recognition beats deliberation' side of NDM: tasks where verbal thinking hurts people. In three of six task types, chain of thought (CoT) also hurts models.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning: GPT-4o zero-shot 87.5% vs CoT 64.4% (-23.1, p<0.0001); o1-preview 57.7% vs GPT-4o zero-shot 94.0% on a subset (-36.3 pts); Claude 3 Opus 70.7 to 62.7; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.9 vs 67.7 (no drop).
limits: Models and humans do not share a mechanism; three of six archetypes showed no consistent drop. Task set chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 (no forced deliberation). Gives a list of task types where slow thinking should be skipped: pattern learning, face-like recognition, exception-heavy rules.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths (2025) Mind Your Step (by Step): CoT can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse (ICML 2025)
finding: Face recognition from descriptions (a recognition task): CoT lowers accuracy in all six multimodal models.
limits: Synthetic dataset of 500 problems; strongest model near ceiling.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that forces verbal analysis can erase recognition ability. Mode choice (fast vs analytic) matters.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths (2025) Mind Your Step (by Step): CoT can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse (ICML 2025)
finding: Learning labels in the presence of exceptions: CoT makes models need many more rounds.
numbers: GPT-4o rounds to learn: direct 2.9, CoT 12.5 (+331%, p<.0001); Claude 3.5 Sonnet 2.3 vs 6.4; Claude 3 Opus 2.4 vs 5.5. GPT-4o with CoT often never fully learned the labels in 15 rounds.
limits: Artificial rule task, not field decisions.
agent_relevance: Rule-based reasoning latches onto the general rule and ignores exceptions. This is the analytic-mode failure that RPD's case matching is meant to avoid.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases), arXiv:2212.05206
finding: Older GPT-3 models fall for intuitive wrong answers on Cognitive Reflection Test tasks and semantic illusions, as humans do. ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 mostly do not.
numbers: 150 CRT tasks: correct 5% for GPT-3-davinci-003, 38% humans, 59% ChatGPT-3.5, 96% ChatGPT-4. Intuitive wrong responses: 80% davinci-003, 55% humans, 15% ChatGPT-3.5, 0% ChatGPT-4. Human CRT correct 38% vs 41% in the original study.
limits: Trap tasks where intuition is wrong by design. Says nothing about tasks where intuition is right (Klein's setting).
agent_relevance: Models are 'hyperrational' on trap tasks. The useful NDM question is the opposite: when is fast recognition right? Liu et al. test that.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS), arXiv:2206.14576
finding: GPT-3 matches humans on classic vignette decisions but breaks on small changes and shows no directed exploration.
numbers: 12 of 12 standard vignettes answered correctly or with human-like mistakes; adversarial rewordings led it astray; it outperformed humans in a multi-armed bandit; it failed causal-reasoning tasks.
limits: GPT-3 (2022); vignettes may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Recognising familiar scenarios is easy for models because they were seen; novel perturbations break it. Test our agent on perturbed cases.

source: Lamparth, Corso, Ganz, Mastro, Schneider, Trinkunas (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences Between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations, arXiv:2403.03407
finding: Real experts versus LLMs in a high-stakes, time-pressed command setting (an NDM-type domain). Overall choices overlap, details differ.
numbers: 214 national security experts in a fictional U.S.-China Taiwan-strait crisis game. LLMs: gpt-3.5-turbo-16k, gpt-4-1106-preview, gpt-4o. No significant difference for about half of the chosen actions; LLMs more aggressive on some moves.
limits: Fictional scenario; humans in teams, LLMs simulated team dialogue. Dialogue length of 3 chunks chosen for the final comparison.
agent_relevance: Model decisions are near expert on common actions but diverge in the tails. Do not use the model as a proxy expert without a check.

source: Lamparth, Corso, Ganz, Mastro, Schneider, Trinkunas (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences Between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations, arXiv:2403.03407
finding: Simulated team dialogue was low quality and unnaturally harmonious; persona prompts did not change results.
numbers: No significant difference between LLM simulations when players were described as 'strict pacifists' or 'aggressive sociopaths'. Simulating dialogue before the decision shifts aggressiveness, with effects that differ by model (GPT-4o more aggressive with longer dialogue).
limits: Single scenario.
agent_relevance: Persona and role prompts do not give real variety (G4). Matches our rule: no persona voters.

source: Rivera, Mukobi, Reuel, Lamparth, Smith, Schneider (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making, arXiv:2401.03408
finding: Eight nation agents, each an LLM taking up to three actions a day with chain-of-thought, plus a world-model LLM. All five tested models escalated, unpredictably, with rare nuclear use.
numbers: Models include GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 2, Llama-2 (70B) Chat; five in total. Escalation scores come from the authors' scoring framework. Reasons cited deterrence and first-strike.
limits: Simulation, not real experts. The escalation score is the authors' own design.
agent_relevance: In sequential crisis decisions an unchecked fast model drifts toward escalation. It needs expectancy monitoring against outcomes, as in RPD.

source: Gullstrand Heander, Soderberg, Rydenfalt (2025) Code Review as Decision-Making, arXiv:2507.09637
finding: Think-aloud study of code review finds an orientation phase then an analytical phase, which the authors link to recognition-primed decision-making.
numbers: 10 participants, 34 code reviews. The model has decisions such as comment, find more information, vote, run locally, verify CI.
limits: Qualitative; small N; human reviewers, not models.
agent_relevance: A human template for agent code-review loops: orient by recognition, then analyse only if a cue says so.

source: Tzanis & Klontzas (2025) System 1 agents: a method for local, reliable and fast agentic AI, arXiv:2611.21053
finding: An agent that picks tools by one-pass multiple-choice answers (no text generation) beat local LLM agents. The name borrows 'System 1'; the abstract makes no link to RPD or Kahneman.
numbers: 1,952 requests, 157 biomedical tools. Best System 1 agent 97.0% correct tool or correct decline vs best of 18 LLM-agent settings 95.2%. Arguments filled for 97.0% of 6,056 values. Invented content 0% vs 5.5-19.7% of LLM calls.
limits: Tool selection only, a narrow recognition-like task. Reading it as 'recognition' is my interpretation, not the authors'.
agent_relevance: Pattern: use constrained single-pass recognition for routing and generation only where needed. Fits our code-decides, model-fills split.

source: Binz et al. (2025) Centaur: a foundation model of human cognition, arXiv:2410.20268
finding: A language model fine-tuned on human choice data predicts held-out participants better than cognitive models, across 160 experiments.
numbers: Psych-101: more than 60,000 participants, over 10,000,000 choices, 160 experiments.
limits: Abstract page only. Lab tasks; no NDM or field tasks named in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Training toward human choices is outside our scope (no training), but shows how far lab-task modelling goes without field tasks.

source: Albert & Billinger (2024) Reproducing and Extending Experiments in Behavioral Strategy with LLMs, arXiv:2410.06932
finding: LLM agents reproduce search behaviour of a human lab experiment; more forward-looking simulated thoughts go with more exploitation over exploration.
numbers: The abstract gives no numbers.
limits: Abstract page only. Lab task.
agent_relevance: Reasoning text can be read as simulated prospection, but the link to behaviour is correlational.

source: Search result: Frontiers in AI 2025 article on judgment and decision-making research for LLM evaluation (frai.2025.1592399)
finding: Argues human judgment and decision research can inform LLM evaluation. A general argument, not an RPD test.
numbers: None read.
limits: Seen only as a search-result title and summary; not opened.
agent_relevance: Possible source for evaluation design. Low priority.

source: Negative search result: no study found testing LLM premortem, Critical Decision Method or RPD with firefighters, military or emergency commanders
finding: arXiv search for 'recognition-primed' returned only the code review paper; 'naturalistic decision making' returned 5 papers, one with LLMs (Mainali). Web search found only practitioner posts on premortem prompts.
numbers: arXiv 'recognition-primed': 1 result (2507.09637). 'naturalistic decision making': 5 results (2510.06093 the only LLM one). 'data-frame' sensemaking: 2 results (2504.15894 and one unrelated chart paper).
limits: Phrase search limits. The arXiv API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited during this run, so coverage is partial. HFES, NDM conference and JCEDM venues not searched.
agent_relevance: The evidence on LLM-for-NDM is thin: one controlled test (Kopka & Feufel). Treat all RPD-prompt claims as [S] single source.

source: Practitioner premortem prompts for LLMs (blog and skill-listing pages, via search)
finding: Many guides recommend asking a model to imagine the plan failed and explain why (Klein's premortem). No controlled measurement found.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Anecdotal; not opened.
agent_relevance: Premortem is already used in agent skills but unmeasured. Worth a small test of our own.
